title: Beyond the basics (learned in practice)
summary: Network waits and mocking, a first API check, and accessibility and visual comparisons. These go past basic tests; every example was run on public demo sites.

lessons.title: Network waits and mocking at a reader's level
keyPoints: Start `waitForResponse` before the action, and only for a request that really happens.
`page.route` plus `route.fulfill` replaces a server response; register the route before the call.
Mock failures and third parties; do not mock the path you are trying to prove.
A mock proves the front end's handling, not the server's behaviour.
lessons.interviewAngle: If asked about mocking, say what you understand and what it can hide. Interviewers like the line "a mocked test does not prove the integration". This goes beyond basic tests: say it was learned in practice on a demo site, not used at work.

exercises.prompt: Why create the `waitForResponse` promise before the click or navigation?
choices: The click would be blocked otherwise
The response might arrive before listening starts and be missed
exercises.explanation: A promise created after the action may start listening too late.

exercises.prompt: Which is a good reason to mock a response?
choices: To check the app shows a clear error when the server returns 500
To prove the main shift-request path works end to end
exercises.explanation: Server errors are hard to trigger for real, and the check is about front-end handling.

exercises.prompt: Which `page` method intercepts requests matching a URL pattern? (Method name only.)
exercises.explanation: `page.route(pattern, handler)`; inside the handler `route.fulfill(...)` sends your response.

exercises.prompt: A test waits for `waitForResponse` after clicking a link on a site that changes pages in the browser without a request. What happens?
choices: It waits until the timeout and fails, because no matching response occurs
exercises.explanation: I hit this on playwright.dev: the wait ran to the 30 second test timeout.

exercises.prompt: A product owner asks whether you can test the screen shown when the dispatch server is down. Explain how you would do it with Playwright, and what the test does and does not prove.
exercises.answer: I would intercept the call the page makes to the shifts endpoint with page.route, registered before navigation, and fulfil it with a 500 status or abort it. Then I load the page and assert that the user sees a clear error message and a way to retry. It proves the front end handles a failed response sensibly. It does not prove the real server behaves that way, or that monitoring notices, so it complements, not replaces, testing the real integration.
rubric: Uses page.route with fulfill or abort
Registers the route before the page loads
States what is not proved (real server)

lessons.title: A first API check with the request fixture
keyPoints: The `request` fixture sends HTTP calls without a browser and uses your config's baseURL.
Assert the exact status, then fields with `toMatchObject`; await `res.json()`.
Use API calls to create test data quickly and to confirm results after a UI action.
Get real endpoints, auth and a test environment from the team.
lessons.interviewAngle: A "have you tested APIs?" question deserves an honest scope: you can do a basic status and field check; at work your testing was UI and UAT, with SQL for data checks. Playwright API testing was learned in practice, not used at work.

choices: That the status is in the 200 to 299 range
That the body is valid JSON
exercises.explanation: For a create call you should also assert the specific status, such as 201.

exercises.prompt: Why use `toMatchObject` on a JSON body?
choices: It checks the named fields and ignores extra ones, so added fields do not break the test
It checks every field including unknown ones
exercises.explanation: It keeps the test focused on the contract that matters.

exercises.prompt: Which test argument gives you a browserless HTTP client? (One word.)
What is a sensible use of an API call in a UI-focused suite?
choices: Guessing endpoints from the browser address bar
Creating an open shift quickly so the UI test starts from known data
exercises.explanation: Setup by API is faster and less fragile than clicking through setup screens.

exercises.prompt: Write a Playwright API test that GETs `/api/shifts/1042` (baseURL is configured) and checks a 200 status, `status` equal to `filled`, and that `pharmacy_id` is a number. Say what you would ask the dev team before running it against a shared environment.
rubric: Uses the request fixture with a relative URL
Asks about environment, auth and test data

lessons.title: Accessibility and visual checks: what they are
keyPoints: Axe scans catch some accessibility issues (contrast, landmarks); they do not prove a page is accessible.
`toMatchAriaSnapshot` compares the accessibility tree of an element.
`toHaveScreenshot` fails on its first run while it writes the baseline; baselines are per platform.
Use visual tests sparingly, on stable elements.
lessons.interviewAngle: If these are mentioned in a job post, say you know what they are and have run them on a demo, not that you run them at work. Offer the limit too: scans are partial and baselines are platform-specific. This goes beyond basic tests: say it was learned in practice on a demo site, not used at work.

exercises.prompt: What happens the first time `toHaveScreenshot('header.png')` runs and no baseline exists?
choices: It sends the image to Azure
It fails and writes the baseline image; the next run compares against it
It passes and ignores the image
exercises.explanation: I ran it: 'A snapshot doesn't exist ... writing actual', then a pass on run two.

exercises.prompt: Why might a screenshot baseline made on a Windows laptop fail in the Linux pipeline?
choices: Screenshots are not supported in CI
Baseline names and pixel rendering are per platform, so fonts and rendering differ
exercises.explanation: The default file name contains the platform, and rendering differs by OS.

exercises.prompt: An axe scan returns no violations. What can you say?
choices: The page has no violations that the automated rules detect; manual checks are still needed
exercises.explanation: Automated rules cover only part of accessibility.

exercises.prompt: Which axe rule id appeared on the TodoMVC demo for text that is hard to read against its background? (id as printed, e.g. color-contrast.)

A hiring manager asks whether you have done accessibility or visual testing. Give an honest answer of about 80 words that states what you have actually done, what you understand, and one limit of each.
exercises.answer: I haven't used either at work; my automation was basic end-to-end tests. I have run both on a public demo site to learn them. An axe scan flagged colour contrast and landmark problems, which showed me it finds some issues quickly, but it cannot judge whether labels make sense, so manual checks are still needed. A screenshot comparison fails on its first run while it saves the baseline, and baselines differ per operating system, so they need care in a pipeline. I'd happily build on that.
rubric: States clearly it was not used at work
Describes what axe found or does
Names a limit of screenshot baselines
